author: Tertullian
occasion: Tertullian offers a catechetical and disciplinary explanation of the Lord's Prayer and of Christian prayer practice, correcting what he regards as superstitious or unscriptural customs that have arisen in the churches.
argument: Tertullian presents the Lord's Prayer as a complete summary of the gospel and the model of all Christian prayer. He expounds each petition in turn, showing how it teaches faith, holiness, submission to God's will, hope for the kingdom, dependence on Christ the daily bread, confession of sins, and deliverance from temptation and evil. He then addresses the conditions and customs of prayer: the need for peace with brethren, purity of heart, clean hands, modest posture and voice, the veiling of virgins, kneeling, times of prayer, and the kiss of peace. He concludes that Christian prayer is the spiritual sacrifice that has replaced the old offerings, and that it is powerful for every good work.

outline.move: Christ established a new form of prayer for the new covenant, and the Lord's Prayer is a summary of the whole gospel.
The address 'Our Father' honors God, confesses faith, and recognizes the Church as mother.
The petition 'hallowed be your name' asks that God's name be sanctified in us and in all people.
'Your will be done' asks for strength to obey God's will, following Christ's example of endurance.
'Your kingdom come' expresses the Christian's eager longing for the end of the age and the coming reign of God.
'Give us this day our daily bread' is understood spiritually of Christ, the bread of life, and teaches reliance on God for necessities.
'Forgive us our debts' is a confession of sin that requires us likewise to forgive our debtors.
'Lead us not into temptation' asks God not to allow us to be led into temptation by the devil, and 'deliver us from evil' interprets it.
The brevity of the Lord's Prayer comprehends all the duties and teachings of the prophets, gospels, and apostles.
After the prescribed prayer, believers may add petitions suited to their own circumstances.
Prayer must be offered in peace, with any discord or offense against a brother first resolved.
Prayer requires a mind free not only from anger but from every disturbance, since the Spirit receives only what is like himself.
True cleanliness of hands is moral purity, not the superstitious washing of hands before prayer.
Christians lift and spread out their hands in prayer, confessing Christ and his passion.
Praying with cloaks removed is a vain, unscriptural custom borrowed from pagan practice.
Sitting down after prayer is another groundless custom, irreverent before the living God.
Prayer should be offered with modest posture, lowered voice, and humility, since God hears the heart, not the voice.
Those fasting should not withhold the kiss of peace after prayer, except where it would reveal their fast.
On station days believers should not abstain from the eucharistic prayers, since receiving the Lord's body does not dissolve their station.
Peter, speaking with the same spirit as Paul, prescribes modesty in women's dress and adornment.
The question is raised whether virgins ought to be veiled, since Paul named 'women' rather than 'virgins.'
Tertullian argues at length that 'women' includes virgins, and that virgins, especially those betrothed, must be veiled.
Kneeling is required on all days except the Lord's Day and Pentecost, and especially on fasts and stations.
The command to pray in every place applies wherever opportunity or necessity allows, as the apostles showed in prison and at sea.
The third, sixth, and ninth hours are fitting times for prayer, and prayer should also precede meals and bathing.
A brother or stranger entering one's home should not be sent away without prayer, and neither host nor guest should take earthly refreshment before heavenly.
The more diligent add 'Alleluia' and psalms to their prayers, and this enriched prayer is offered as a rich sacrifice to God.
Christian prayer is the spiritual sacrifice that has replaced the old sacrifices, offered by true worshippers in spirit and truth.
Prayer is powerful for every good work, and all creation, even the angels and the Lord himself, prays.

cast.name: Tertullian
cast.who: The author, a Christian teacher in Carthage writing to instruct fellow believers.

cast.name: Jesus Christ
cast.who: The Lord, who taught the Lord's Prayer and is the model and object of Christian prayer.

cast.name: John the Baptist
cast.who: The forerunner who taught his disciples to pray, but whose work gave way to Christ.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: The lawgiver who asked God his name and received a different name from the one revealed in the Son.

cast.name: Peter
cast.who: The apostle who asked about forgiveness and whose practice of praying at the sixth hour is cited.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle whose teaching on women's dress and veiling is cited.

cast.name: Eve
cast.who: The first woman, called 'woman' while still unmarried, showing the term includes virgins.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first man, who with Eve covered himself once he knew.

cast.name: Rebecca
cast.who: The matriarch who veiled herself upon seeing her betrothed Isaac.

cast.name: Daniel
cast.who: The prophet who prayed three times a day, an example of Israelite discipline.

cast.name: Hermas
cast.who: Author of the Shepherd, cited for sitting on a bed after prayer, which Tertullian says is not a rule.

cast.name: Pilate
cast.who: The governor who washed his hands at the Lord's betrayal, an example Christians should not imitate.

cast.name: Isaiah
cast.who: The prophet whose cry is invoked against unclean hands.

cast.name: Jonah
cast.who: The prophet whose prayer rose from the belly of the sea monster.

cast.name: Cain
cast.who: The first murderer, whose vengeance was reckoned sevenfold.

cast.name: Lamech
cast.who: The descendant of Cain, whose vengeance was reckoned seventy-sevenfold.

cast.name: Joseph
cast.who: The patriarch who told his brothers not to be angry on the way.

cast.name: Carpus
cast.who: The man with whom Paul left his cloak, mentioned in the debate over praying without a cloak.

key_terms.sense: Prayer, especially the Lord's Prayer and Christian prayer as a spiritual sacrifice
The teaching, training, and rule of Christian life and worship
Pertaining to the Holy Spirit or the spiritual realm, as opposed to carnal or earthly
Faith in God and Christ, especially as expressed and exercised in prayer
The offering made to God, now understood as prayer offered in spirit and truth
A day of fasting and prayer, drawn from military watch-duty
The kiss of peace exchanged among Christians at prayer
To cover the head, especially of women and virgins in worship
Woman, argued by Tertullian to include virgins as well as married women
An unmarried woman or one consecrated to God, whose veiling is debated
Temptation or testing, especially by the devil
Debts, understood as sins that require forgiveness
Daily bread, understood spiritually as Christ the bread of life
Confession of sins, especially in the petition for forgiveness

scripture: Tertullian quotes from the Old Testament in Latin, generally following the Septuagint tradition as mediated by the Old Latin versions. He refers to Genesis, Isaiah, and the Psalms by their traditional names. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint/Vulgate system. Modern citations should use standard English Bible names (e.g., Genesis, Isaiah, Psalms) and note where Septuagint/Vulgate Psalm numbering differs from the Hebrew.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is not stated in the text; it is placed in Tertullian's early orthodox period, roughly 198–204 AD, based on external evidence.
The precise identity of the 'blessed ones' (benedicti) addressed is not specified beyond being fellow Christians.
Whether Tertullian is responding to a particular local controversy or a general set of customs is not explicitly stated.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Paul, source_forms: ['Paulus'], who: The apostle whose teaching on women's dress and veiling is cited.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Paul is never named in the source text. Tertullian refers to 'apostolus' in section 20 ('post sanctissimum apostolum') and section 22 ('eodem spiritu, quo Paulus'), but the name 'Paulus' does not appear. The source forms should be ['apostolus'] or empty, and the description should note he is referred to as 'the apostle' without being named.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Scripture (1 Corinthians), how_marked: Quoted with 'inquit' but without naming Paul as the speaker, sections: ['22']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: naturam ipsam docere uelandum feminis esse, quae capillum pro tegumento et ornamento mulieribus assignarit
_unresolved_facts.fix: The passage in section 22 does not use 'inquit' for the nature argument. The 'inquit' in section 22 appears with 'omnis mulier adorans et prophetans intecto capite dedecorat caput suum' (quoting 1 Corinthians 11:5), but this is marked as Scripture/Christ, not specifically '1 Corinthians.' More importantly, the 'naturam ipsam docere' argument is not introduced with 'inquit' but as Tertullian's own argument from nature. The voice entry should be corrected or removed.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Jesus Christ (responding to Peter's question), how_marked: Peter's question is narrated, and the Lord's response 'septuagies septies' is quoted with 'inquit', sections: ['7']
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: et cum interrogasset Petrus, si septies remittendum esset fratri, immo, inquit, septuagies septies
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'inquit' here does not clearly mark Jesus as the speaker; it could be Tertullian commenting. The passage is introduced with 'inquit' after 'immo' without explicit speaker identification. The brief should note the speaker attribution is implicit, not explicit.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Opponents (those who allow virgins unveiled), how_marked: Introduced by 'inquiunt', sections: ['21']
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'inquiunt' appears in section 21, but it refers to the arguments of those who allow virgins to be unveiled ('qui enim uirginibus indulgent capitis immunitatem'). However, the brief's description is accurate. Actually checking again: the 'inquiunt' is at 'potuit enim, inquiunt' - this is the opponents speaking. This seems correct. Removing this problem.
